# The Moonshot {#sec-moonshot}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers."*
>
> — Richard Hamming, *Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers* (1962) [@Hamming1962NumericalMethods]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Richard Hamming, a pioneer in computer science, argued that
computing should yield insight rather than raw data. The distinction matters
here. AI-assisted architecture should help architects ask better questions,
test alternatives, explain mechanisms, and defend decisions. Producing more
candidates is useful only when it improves that work.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What would it take to build an AI-assisted capability that carries compact
system intent through real system-and-chip design to a supported architecture
result, rather than merely generating artifacts faster?
:::

Computer architecture has repeatedly expanded what engineers could design by
advancing its methods as well as its devices. The lasting advances did more than
automate a local step. They gave architects better abstractions, repeatable ways
to turn those abstractions into design artifacts, and checks that exposed bad
results. That history sets the standard for judging AI-assisted design.

AI is a possibility, not an assumed necessity or a guarantee of better
architecture. Learned methods can work with less structured information,
propose and screen alternatives, and coordinate actions across tools. Those
abilities are worth testing, but they do not make the resulting artifacts
correct, physically realizable, or architecturally useful.

That standard defines an ambitious, testable moonshot. Could a complete design
system carry compact system intent through alternatives, tools, measurements,
and checks until the work supports a hardware-and-software architecture result?
The target is not autonomous prompt-to-chip generation. The moonshot's added
complexity and cost are justified only if the complete approach improves the
architecture work.

The Lighthouse request grounds the moonshot in a low-power mobile XR subsystem.
Its short statement hides a full-stack architecture study across workloads,
software, hardware, and physical implementation. It lets us ask whether AI
changes architecture practice or merely accelerates a local task.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Define the Architecture 2.0 moonshot and AI-assisted design capabilities.
- Translate compact system intent into explicit cross-stack architecture specifications.
- Distinguish generated artifacts from verifiable architecture results.
- Evaluate architecture quality and design efficacy as independent tests.
:::

## When New Methods Changed What Engineers Could Design

Several familiar transitions show how a new method can widen architecture
practice. The Mead--Conway VLSI methodology[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01] joined
abstractions and design rules to tools, fabrication access, and teaching
[@MeadConway1980VLSI]. Reduced-instruction-set computing reshaped the
hardware--software contract around a small set of principles that architects
could test quantitatively [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC]. Logic synthesis made it
practical to transform register-transfer-level descriptions into gate-level
implementations, while timing analysis and equivalence checking exposed bad
outputs [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization; @Formality]. In each case, the
idea became consequential because other engineers could apply, inspect, and
improve the method built around it.

[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01]: **VLSI complexity (origin)**: Early-1980s frontier microprocessors held about $10^4$ to $10^5$ transistors, and by 2021 frontier chips held tens of billions [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData]. Mead and Conway answered that outgrowth of transistor-level practice with higher-level abstractions, design rules, and fabrication access that a course could teach and a community could share.

These transformations used different technical mechanisms, but each widened
the unit of design that engineers could express and made the resulting object
checkable through shared rules, tools, or measurements
(@fig-design-method-progression).

![**New design methods widened what engineers could express and check.** Established advances joined an input abstraction to a larger design object and to the checks or infrastructure that made the transformation dependable. AI-assisted architecture is shown separately as a prospective system for carrying system intent and current project state to a supported architecture result through existing tools and checks.](images/F1d-design-method-progression){#fig-design-method-progression width="100%" fig-alt="Historical progression through Mead-Conway design rules and abstractions, the RISC hardware-software contract, RTL logic synthesis, and reusable hardware generators. Each established method connects an input abstraction to a design object and a dependable check or infrastructure. A separate prospective case shows an AI-assisted design system connecting system intent and current project state through existing tools and checks to a supported comparison or finding with stated alternatives and limits; the result may reject a candidate or retain the reference design."}

The established rows extend from shared design rules to parameterized hardware
generators [@Izraelevitz2017Chisel], and each pairs a wider design object with
external checks. The prospective row is different because its stronger claim
remains unproven. It asks whether a design system can connect broader intent and
current project state to a supported architecture result without weakening the
tools and checks on which that result depends. This is neither an inevitable
next stage nor a prompt-to-chip pipeline.

Measured against those transitions, generating more code, RTL, or design
proposals would be useful, but it would not by itself constitute a new design
method. The harder problem is to help architects carry intent across workloads,
software, hardware, and physical implementation while
reducing the human effort required to explore and check alternatives. We call
that long-range target an *architecture moonshot*.

> **Architecture moonshot.** An architecture moonshot is a difficult,
> long-term target that existing tools and design practice cannot yet address
> end to end. It seeks a major improvement in how architects turn system and
> chip design questions into supported results and decisions. Advances in AI,
> data, or tools must make at least part of the target practical to investigate
> without implying that the whole problem has been solved.

An architecture moonshot becomes credible only when an important architecture
problem, a substantial change in design practice, and an enabling advance that
makes meaningful progress possible coincide (@fig-moonshot-venn).

![**A moonshot becomes testable only when all three conditions hold.** A major architecture challenge and a proposed change in design practice require a demonstrated advance in AI, data, or tools that makes meaningful progress practical.](images/F1c-moonshot-venn){#fig-moonshot-venn width="85%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram showing an architecture moonshot at the intersection of a grand architecture challenge, a substantial change in design practice, and an enabling advance in AI, data, or tools."}

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

Each condition rules out a different failure. A difficult problem without a
new method remains an unsolved problem. A proposed method without a demonstrated
enabling capability remains an aspiration. An enabling advance with no
architecture problem behind it remains a capability demonstration. The program must show that an
advance in AI, data, or tools makes a meaningful part of the target practical,
rather than infer that capability from the ambition alone.

Explicitly Parallel Instruction Computing (EPIC), the basis of Itanium, makes
the risk of a moonshot dependency concrete. It shifted much of the scheduling
responsibility to the compiler and made compiler-exposed parallelism central
to the architecture [@SchlanskerRau2000EPIC].

::: {.callout-war-story title="EPIC shows why a moonshot must name its dependency"}
**The claim.** EPIC exposed instruction-level parallelism in the ISA so
the compiler could schedule operations explicitly.

**The gap.** The expected benefit depended on the compiler finding and
scheduling enough useful parallelism despite control flow, aliasing, memory
behavior, and the available software path.

**The lesson.** A moonshot can fail when it depends on a capability whose
limits become clear only after large commitments. AI-assisted architecture
faces the same risk if it assumes that plausible generation will become
physically valid system design without demonstrating the required knowledge,
tool use, and checks.
:::

The lesson is not to avoid ambitious targets. It is to state what capability
the target depends on and what result would challenge that assumption. To test
that dependency with the Lighthouse, we first need to place AI within
established design automation and name the components that might perform the work.

## AI as Design Automation

Design automation uses models, algorithms, and tools to turn design intent
into artifacts and results under explicit constraints. Logic synthesis,
parameterized generators, design-space search, and verification already
automate substantial parts of architecture work. Researchers and engineers
are adding learned methods to that practice, from design-space exploration to
physical placement
[@WangEtAl2026AgentDSE; @MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. These methods extend
design automation rather than replace the methods and tools that already make
designs executable and checkable.

In this book, *AI* names a field and a set of learned techniques, not a
component. These techniques include prediction, generation, optimization, and
other task-specific uses. An AI-assisted system can combine them with
conventional analysis and design tools.

A model's inputs, outputs, and use determine the work it can perform. A
*learned model* fits part of its behavior from examples rather than having every
rule written explicitly. A *predictor* estimates a property that is expensive
or unavailable to measure directly. A *generator* proposes an artifact or
design candidate. An *optimizer* chooses among alternatives to improve a stated
objective. *Retrieval* finds relevant information in an identified body of
material. A canonical AI definition describes an *agent* through perception of
an environment and action within it
[@RussellNorvig2020AIMA].
This book uses a stricter operational threshold for architecture assistance:
an agent takes actions in an environment, observes what the environment
returns, and can change its next action from that feedback. A model that
answers one prompt is not necessarily an agent, and a fixed script is not an
agent simply because it calls several tools.

These distinctions describe capabilities, not authority. Generation, prediction, and
optimization are method families; proposing a candidate, estimating a
consequence, selecting an experiment, repairing an artifact, and checking a
property are roles. One method can perform several roles, and a role can be
filled by a learned method, a conventional algorithm, a design tool, or an
architect. The assigned role, not the AI label, determines what the component
must produce and how its output must be checked.

AI in architecture also has a longer history than recent generative systems.
Researchers have used learned predictors, surrogate models, reinforcement
learning, and autotuning for branch prediction, prefetching, controllers, and
design-space exploration [@ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture; @JimenezLin2001Perceptron;
@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling; @ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @AnselEtAl2014OpenTuner]. Recent language and
generative models broaden the kinds of information and artifacts that methods
can work with [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @HeEtAl2024ChatEDA]. The continuity
matters. Some learned mechanisms, such as branch predictors, operate inside the
systems being designed. Other learned methods, such as surrogate models and
autotuners, help conduct the design work. This book focuses on the second use.
Architecture already combines human judgment with models, scripts, generators,
simulators, compilers, synthesis, optimization, and verification. The new
question is where learned methods improve that complete practice.

Applying these methods to architecture runs into several immediate limits.
Project-specific specifications, implementation data, and tool results may
not appear in public training corpora; ChipNeMo, for example, relies on
proprietary chip-design data and internal evaluation [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo].
The feedback needed to reject a candidate can also be expensive. BOOM-Explorer
reports hours for one sample in its documented implementation flow
[@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer], and an industry survey reports that verification
accounts for a large share of project engineering effort
[@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Repeated model inference consumes compute
and adds latency of its own. Inference benchmarks explicitly measure latency
and throughput [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. Data preparation, tool feedback,
verification, and inference all belong in the total work of an AI-assisted
study. Candidate generation or ranking is only part of that work.

## The Lighthouse Request

The Lighthouse starts with a short product request. Expanding it exposes work
across the full design stack and makes the difficulty of AI-assisted
architecture concrete. Data and evaluation cost remain part of the study, but
the architect must first determine what the request actually requires. The same
request serves as the running example throughout the book.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse request"}
Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an XRBench-class
real-time mobile XR workload. Realize it as a vector-capable CPU, accelerator,
or SoC block under a 3\ W TDP target in a 3\ nm-class LP mobile process, and
return a design-space report with evidence and rejected alternatives.
:::

We call this the *Lighthouse prompt*. Here XR means extended reality, TDP means
thermal design power, and LP identifies a low-power process. XRBench is a public
suite of mobile XR workloads rather than a complete product specification
[@KwonEtAl2023XRBench]. The prompt's scale deliberately exposes the architecture
work that a smaller generation task would hide. It provides a long-term target
for judging progress toward the full challenge.

Mobile XR makes that target useful because it combines tight latency, thermal,
and energy constraints with cross-layer behavior. A design cannot optimize one
kernel or block while ignoring the software pipeline, memory system, or
user-visible frame deadline [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR].

Industrial integration raises the standard again. An accelerator in a
system-on-chip (SoC) is not a clean-sheet island. It must connect to existing
intellectual property through protocols such as AMBA AXI.[^fn-axi-c01] A
candidate that improves power, performance, and area (PPA) but violates an AXI
handshake is not an integrable design.

[^fn-axi-c01]: **AMBA AXI**: An Arm-defined on-chip interface protocol with separate channels and strict valid-ready handshake requirements [@Arm2020AXI]. A block that violates the protocol cannot be integrated into a system that depends on that interface, no matter how good its isolated power and performance numbers look.

The word *prompt* is intentionally modest. A request or prompt expresses
compact intent. Requirements interpret its obligations and identify choices
that remain open. A specification fixes enough behavior, interfaces,
workloads, software semantics, constraints, and acceptance checks to make
implementation testable. A study plan then fixes the reference design,
alternatives, tools, budget, and stopping conditions for a particular
comparison. The Lighthouse request is not yet a specification.
"XRBench-class," "3\ W," "3\ nm-class," and the permitted compute organizations
still require versioned workloads, software paths, reference designs, process
assumptions, and checks. The architect must make those open choices explicit
before the request can guide real design work, deciding which interpretation
becomes part of the specification and what result would satisfy it.

The prompt does not imply a single model or invocation. Answering it takes a
memory trace collected from a fixed XRBench workload and configuration, a
compiler that can target the proposed organization, a
simulator, a synthesis run against a low-power library, and reviewers who can
qualify which results support the recommendation. This book studies that
complete human-plus-technical workflow, not the fluency of one generated
response.

Studying that workflow requires explicit meanings for *architecture* and
*architect*. Architecture is more than a microarchitecture, block diagram, or
chip artifact.

> **Architecture.** Architecture is the hardware and software contract and system organization turning workload intent and technology constraints into a defensible system design. It includes the instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture, memory, interconnects, accelerators, chiplets, compiler and runtime interfaces, and deployment model.

> **Architect.** The architect is responsible for the architecture
> recommendation within the project's decision structure. The architect frames
> the problem, chooses abstractions, sets the evidence standard, integrates
> cross-layer results, and forms the supported technical recommendation.
> Specialists qualify measurements and checks and own technical signoffs in
> their domains. A separately named commitment authority decides whether the
> architecture advances to the next consequential transition. One person may
> hold more than one role, but the project must identify each responsibility
> and approval right.
> Methods can contribute candidates and analysis without assuming these
> responsibilities.

Applied to the Lighthouse, these definitions require a hardware-and-software
result rather than a chip artifact alone. A particular investigation must still
fix the workload version and deadline, architecture and software path,
reference design, process libraries, operating assumptions, tools, budget,
stopping conditions, implementation constraints, verification obligations, and
measurements. Changing a fixed condition changes the challenge; resolving an
open choice makes it executable. Those choices make the comparison possible,
but they are not themselves the architecture. The architect must be able to
defend how they support the comparison and technical recommendation.

## From a Few Lines to a Full-Stack Problem {#sec-intent-vs-spec}

The Lighthouse request spans the entire stack because its compact wording
conceals two levels of work. Its phrases must first become architecture
requirements and then a tool-connected comparison that can support a technical
recommendation (@fig-moonshot-prompt).

![**A compact prompt hides a full architecture study.** The prompt implies architecture requirements and engineering work that must be completed before an architect can form a supported result and technical recommendation.](images/F1-moonshot-stack){#fig-moonshot-prompt width="85%" fig-alt="Stacked diagram with the full Lighthouse prompt at the top, architecture requirements in the middle, and the execution and analysis requirements needed to support an answer at the bottom."}

Architecture requirements do not run a compiler or simulator. The accepted
workload, software, hardware, physical, reliability, and verification
obligations must also connect to represented study state, tools, measurements,
and checks (@fig-moonshot-prompt). Tool results may send the architect back to
revise those obligations. This tool-connected work is hidden behind the prompt;
it is not a prompt-to-chip automation pipeline.

[]{#sec-why-the-prompt-spans-the-stack}

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

Start with the prompt itself. High-level intent first becomes questions and coupled design choices, not a generated chip artifact. The prompt tasks the architect with comparing several compute organizations for a real-time mobile XR workload, all while respecting a 3\ W TDP[^fn-tdp-c01] budget and the limits of an LP process. Individual phrases bound different parts of the study.

[^fn-tdp-c01]: **TDP (thermal design power)**: This book treats the Lighthouse target as a 3\ W sustained thermal envelope that the declared form factor and cooling assumptions must be able to remove, rather than as a peak instantaneous draw.

The phrase "64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem" fixes the word length and
ISA family. Each study must still choose the exact ISA extensions,
ABI[^fn-abi-c01], compiler, runtime, and software contract. The "XRBench-class
real-time mobile XR workload" phrase sets the target environment. The
"accelerator block" provision leaves several compute organizations open for
comparison. The 3\ W target and 3\ nm-class LP process supply hard
physical limits that can rule out an unfeasible proposal. A 3\ W TDP in a
mobile XR form factor requires the study to state its cooling and
skin-temperature assumptions, packaging, signaling, and the share of the power
budget available to the proposed compute subsystem.

[^fn-abi-c01]: **ABI (application binary interface)**: The binary-level agreement on register usage, calling conventions, stack layout, and data alignment that lets separately compiled code interoperate. Adding a custom instruction changes the ISA, but shipping it means the compiler, libraries, and operating system have to agree on the ABI as well, which is why an ISA extension is a software project rather than a hardware edit.

While the prompt asks for a design-space report, the study may also produce software, models, RTL, layouts, prototypes, or a physical chip, depending on the ambition of the claim. The report connects those artifacts and measurements to the proposed design and explains precisely why alternatives were rejected. To test the architect's judgment, the prompt deliberately leaves the accelerator microarchitecture, memory system, software integration, and evaluation tools open.

Turning those choices into a study requires explicit constraints that the
relevant tools can use. Requirement translation already combines profiling,
analytical models, prior designs, design tools, and expert judgment. A product
request such as "we need a low-power AR headset" does not determine a 3\ W TDP,
a particular RISC-V extension, or an L2 capacity on its own. The architect must
derive those study parameters from workload and system evidence.

Learned methods can assist by extracting candidate constraints from requirement documents, relating them to prior designs and public benchmarks, and identifying ambiguities for the architect to resolve. When a prompt asks for a "real-time" workload, a language model might ask whether that means a strict 11 millisecond frame deadline at 90\ Hz, a 20 millisecond motion-to-photon bound, or a 99th-percentile tail-latency target.

This assistance does not remove the architect's formulation work. It may reduce the time spent assembling candidate specifications, while the architect still decides whether the proposed bounds are complete and supported. Before search begins, the accepted constraints should be represented in a form the relevant tools can use, such as a parameterized generator configuration or a sweep specification. Prose alone cannot define the legal design space.

Each fragment of the Lighthouse prompt implies a cluster of architectural
decisions and the checks that could disqualify an answer
(@tbl-moonshot-decomposition). A method may suggest a hardware and software
decomposition. The architect accepts, revises, or rejects that proposed scope
and its coupled interfaces.

| **Prompt fragment** | **Architectural decisions** | **What must be checked** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **XRBench mobile XR** | Workload slice, input distribution, quality-of-service target, latency deadline, memory traffic, software pipeline, and drift assumptions. | Trace source, benchmark version, documented workload-phase selection, and rejection when results over-optimize a single hot loop or miss real-time behavior. |
| **64-bit RISC-V with vector or accelerator option** | ISA boundary, custom extension policy, programming model, compiler/runtime path, library support, and software compatibility. | Correctness, toolchain support, generated-code evidence, portability checks, and rejection of unsupported software semantics. |
| **Compute subsystem** | CPU, vector, or accelerator organization; memory hierarchy and interconnect; system integration; interface compatibility; and relevant reliability or isolation assumptions. | Design-space comparison and rejection of candidates that only win by moving cost, bandwidth, energy, complexity, or risk elsewhere. |
| **3\ W, 3\ nm-class low-power envelope** | Power, voltage and frequency, thermal and area limits, implementation constraints, and the hardware and software interfaces used for power management. | Source, version, and calibration of the power model; physical-design limits such as voltage drop, wire reliability, and timing closure; sensitivity analysis; and rejection criteria for throttling or reliability failures. |
| **Design-space report with evidence and rejected alternatives** | Alternatives, the Pareto frontier (the set of objective outcomes of feasible designs for which no alternative is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on at least one) [@Deb2001MultiObjective], assumptions, uncertainty, verification plan, rejected or failed candidates, and points at which the responsible architect decides whether to continue. | Measurements linked to assumptions and checks, rejected candidates, coverage, reproducible artifacts, and a named person responsible for the recommendation. |

: **A compact prompt hides multiple architecture decisions and independent checks.** The Lighthouse request expands into workload definition, software and ISA contracts, hardware organization, physical feasibility, and the checks that can reject an answer. {#tbl-moonshot-decomposition tbl-colwidths="[18,34,35]"}

The decisions in the table cannot be settled independently. A workload,
software, hardware, or physical choice can change the validity of the others
and the checks that might disqualify an answer. The table therefore expands the
requirements rather than completing the specification. An answer remains
incomplete if it cannot identify its workload slice, software contract,
physical assumptions, supporting observations, and recommendation owner. Any
proposed commitment separately identifies a named authority.

The workload and process phrases require more detail than the compact prompt provides. The XRBench suite supplies a concrete workload anchor rather than a vague application label. End-to-end XR research shows how tightly perception and display stages are coupled, making mobile XR a system-level architecture target rather than a single kernel to optimize [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR]. Learned methods can help here by analyzing dataset distributions to find coverage gaps, complementing profiling, trace analysis, and expert workload judgment. For instance, a method could analyze a memory trace collected from a fixed XRBench workload and configuration, then cluster access patterns to suggest cache hierarchies or local scratchpads for simulation.

The selected benchmark must represent the system claim. Similarly, the process
node is stated as a broad class rather than a named foundry process design kit
(PDK)[^fn-pdk-c01]. Even though 2024 mobile SoCs were publicly described in
3\ nm-class technology [@Apple2024A18Pro; @Apple2024M4], the study must
explicitly name the process, libraries, voltage assumptions, and signoff path. Each
surviving candidate needs the relevant physical-design flow before it can
support a physical-feasibility claim.

[^fn-pdk-c01]: **PDK (process design kit)**: The package for one manufacturing process that supplies device models, design rules, and related data used by implementation tools. The open SKY130 PDK demonstrates that a PDK can be published [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK], but it cannot supply the authorized project-specific information for a different process or commercial tool flow.

The short prompt therefore hides substantial engineering depth. Early studies
may screen candidates against the "3\ W, 3\ nm-class" constraint with
calibrated models or partial implementation. Only a candidate used to support a
physical-feasibility claim must eventually reach the relevant RTL, synthesis,
floorplanning, timing, voltage-drop, leakage, thermal, and signoff checks.
Comparing the RISC-V vector and accelerator alternatives also requires checking
the compiler, runtime, libraries, generated code, and software portability. The
software stack can be the limiting dependency. A novel spatial accelerator is
dead silicon if the compiler cannot be co-adapted to target it. Meeting the
workload and physical requirements takes a design system that
keeps knowledge, tools, and review connected across the full system.

## A Foundation Model for System and Chip Design

Carrying the Lighthouse question across the stack requires more than reusable
model knowledge. The technical system must maintain current project state,
combine learned and conventional methods, connect those methods to compilers,
simulators, implementation tools, and verification, and return results that can
be checked independently of the method that produced the candidate.

The general foundation-model pattern begins with broad training followed by
adaptation across downstream tasks [@BommasaniEtAl2021FoundationModels]. Here,
an *architecture foundation model* is one broadly pretrained learned component
intended for adaptation across multiple architecture tasks.
It may supply reusable prior knowledge, but it does not contain authoritative
live project state and is not a complete design system. The *AI-assisted design
system* is the configured technical ensemble of learned and conventional
components, tools, maintained state, feedback, and checks. The complete
human-plus-technical workflow also includes setup, intervention, review,
repair, budgets, and stopping decisions. The technical system returns
checkable results, the architect forms the technical recommendation, and the
named commitment authority separately decides whether the design advances to
the next consequential transition. A particular problem may use one foundation
model, several specialized models, or no foundation model at all. The moonshot
concerns what this complete workflow can accomplish, not the name or scale of
any one model.

Reusable learning can contribute to several architecture tasks without
replacing the rest of the design system (@fig-foundation-system). Prior
architecture artifacts and results can support one learned component that
adapts to several tasks. The current workload,
constraints, candidate, tool versions, and measurements remain separate in the
current version-controlled project record. That record is authoritative for
what the study used, but its contents still require qualification and can be
wrong.

![**A foundation model is one optional component of the design system.** Reusable architecture knowledge can support a learned component adapted to workload analysis, prediction, generation, or diagnosis. The current project record, conventional methods, compilers, simulators, EDA and formal tools, and independent checks remain part of the larger system. The architecture role supplies intent and constraints, reviews the supported result, and forms a supported technical recommendation. A separate commitment authority decides whether the project advances, holds, or rejects that recommendation.](images/F1a-foundation-system){#fig-foundation-system width="100%" fig-alt="Reusable architecture knowledge feeds an optional architecture foundation model inside an AI-assisted design system. A separate version-controlled project record informs the active architecture tasks and conventional methods. Task outputs reach design tools and checks, which return evidence and update project state. A supported architecture result leaves the technical system for review by the architecture role, which forms a supported technical recommendation for a separate commitment authority."}

For the Lighthouse, the reusable component might help analyze XR workloads,
screen candidate organizations, draft software or RTL, or diagnose a failed
check. The live study, by contrast, supplies the current trace, 3\ W envelope,
candidate identity, and tool and library versions. Those current inputs
determine what the simulators, implementation tools, and verification flows
evaluate; reusable prior knowledge cannot substitute for them.

## An Artifact Is Not an Architecture Result

A request does not become an architecture result in one step. Architecture
work moves from request through requirements, specification, candidate
artifacts, measurements and checks, comparative architecture result, technical
recommendation, and commitment decision. These stages must remain distinct.
An *artifact* is something produced during the work, such as code, RTL, a
model, a layout, a report, or a testbench. A *candidate* is a proposed design
or configuration being compared. A *measurement* or *observation* is
information obtained about a candidate under stated conditions. An
*architecture result* is a supported comparison or finding whose assumptions,
conditions, checks, alternatives, and limits are clear enough to inform a
next architecture action. The architect integrates that result into a
technical recommendation and selects any further study action. The named
commitment authority decides whether the architecture advances to the next
consequential transition. An architecture result can reject every candidate,
support retaining the current design, narrow the question, or conclude that
the available measurements cannot decide.

These distinctions determine how scarce feedback should be allocated. An
architect might begin with a memory-trace slice collected from a fixed XRBench
workload and configuration, together with its software pipeline,
propose vector-width or CPU and accelerator alternatives, and screen them with
a cheap proxy. Compiler, simulator, RTL, and physical-design work can then be
reserved for candidates whose results could alter the next architecture action
or technical recommendation. The selection rule and the claim each check may
support should be stated before the run.

The distance between an artifact and a result is especially large in hardware.
A generator might produce a mathematically elegant instruction extension that
passes behavioral simulation and still fail logic equivalence checking,
design-rule checks, timing, power, or thermal limits in implementation. A
surrogate model[^fn-surrogate-model-c01] can cheaply screen candidates, but a
candidate selected by the surrogate may fail when a more faithful tool exposes
a property the surrogate did not represent. This is the architecture version
of the simulation-to-real problem studied in machine learning
[@TobinEtAl2017DomainRandomization].

[^fn-surrogate-model-c01]: **Surrogate model**: A cheaper approximation of an expensive evaluation that lets a method screen many candidates quickly [@ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. Its score is only a proxy, so a promising candidate still needs a higher-fidelity check before it can support a design decision.

Once a study has measured the affected workload fraction and stated its mapping
assumptions, Amdahl's law supplies an inexpensive rejection bound. An
accelerator that covers 60 percent of the XR pipeline's cycles caps
whole-system speedup at 2.5 times, no matter how fast the block itself becomes
[@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. The arithmetic can reject a claim whose
own profiled coverage cannot support the stated gain before the candidate
consumes a simulator hour. It does not verify the profile, mapping, overlap,
memory behavior, or implementation. The bound must be recomputed if a candidate
changes the covered work or the software path.

The roofline model supplies a second screening bound by relating operational
intensity to peak compute and memory bandwidth [@Williams2009Roofline]. Like
the Amdahl calculation, it is inexpensive only after the study has measured or
declared the inputs and assumptions that define the bound.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The roofline rejects a candidate before the simulator sees it"}
**Context.** The roofline bounds attainable performance once the study has a
candidate-specific operational intensity and the platform's peak compute and
memory bandwidth, which set its machine balance.

**How assistance uses the screen.** Generation can propose legal vector
configurations, prediction can estimate their data-movement risks, and
optimization can choose which configurations merit simulation. A candidate
whose bound is already inadequate need not enter the simulator queue.

**Required conditions and checks.** Operational intensity must reflect the
candidate's mapping, declared memory boundary, and cache or scratchpad
behavior. The study must recompute the bound when those properties change and
must still verify the mapping and resulting design for surviving candidates.

**Takeaway.** The roofline can reject an implausible candidate cheaply; it
cannot establish that the final design works.
:::

Analytical bounds, proxy scores, simulator results, and EDA reports provide
different evidence at sharply different costs. A proxy may rank candidates one
way, a simulator may overturn that ranking, and an EDA run may return timing
paths and congestion rather than a single score. BOOM-Explorer reports that
some implementation evaluations take hours [@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer].
Iterative search may require many trials before it can distinguish better
actions. When the available evaluation capacity cannot cover those trials, a
brute-force approach exceeds the budget. Statistical
overfitting[^fn-overfitting-c01] provides a useful analogy, but the architecture
failure is more specific. Repeated search against a fast proxy can exploit its
omissions or errors, producing apparent gains that disappear when the surviving
candidates reach a higher-fidelity tool.

[^fn-overfitting-c01]: **Overfitting**: The machine-learning failure of fitting the noise of a training sample so closely that performance does not generalize to new data [@HastieTibshiraniFriedman2009Elements]. Proxy exploitation is analogous but not identical; it can occur when search uses omissions or errors in an evaluator even without fitting a statistical model.

Evaluation does not end when a candidate clears its current checks. Hardware
commitments freeze key choices on a much longer timescale than workloads,
compilers, libraries, and learned models evolve. An optimizer cannot safely
specialize a 3\ nm-class accelerator to one static trace without considering
how the workload and software may change before deployment. The architect must
balance specialization with enough programmability to survive that interval.

Even after bounds, proxies, and search narrow the work, their output alone does not prove
whether a compiler assumption holds, whether the measured behavior follows from
the proposed mechanism, or whether the remaining tradeoff supports the next
consequential transition. The study should record the candidates,
assumptions, measurements, checks, and rejections that affect the claim without
requiring every internal model trace. A concise rationale should connect those
proposals, tool results, rejected alternatives, and the recommendation, while
remaining clearly distinct from the measurements themselves. It helps a
reviewer find missing assumptions, contradictions, or conclusions that the
checks do not support. The architect uses the recorded results and rationale to
form the technical recommendation or select the next study action.

A useful result must clear a higher threshold than an artifact. Its measurements
must support a comparison under stated conditions, and the required checks must
support the conclusion. Important alternatives and failures must be recorded,
and the result must be able to inform the next architecture action. Rejecting a
candidate, retaining the current architecture, or choosing a conventional
method can all be useful results.

Useful results do not need to cover the whole Lighthouse challenge. Progress
can close one clearly stated part without claiming an end-to-end answer. A
full-scope result addresses the complete challenge and may still conclude that
no candidate works. That result does not by itself establish the contribution
of any named component or the success of the broader Architecture 2.0 program.
Full Lighthouse success requires a supported design that meets the fixed
conditions and the complete design-space report promised by the prompt,
including the software path, physical constraints, rejected alternatives,
applicable reliability and security properties under the declared fault and
threat models, checks, and a recommendation an independent architect can
examine.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Qualify artifacts before asserting results"}
A candidate, RTL block, report, or tool output is merely an unverified artifact
until qualified by measurements and checks under stated conditions. Never treat
a syntactically valid script or a successful local tool return as evidence that
an architecture should change. A valid architecture result must explicitly
identify the candidate, workload, measurement, check, and bounding conditions.
Only when this verified evidence can inform a specific architecture action does
an artifact become a result.
:::

## An Architecture Result Needs More Than One Score {#sec-efficiency-claims-need-rejectable-loops}

Even if the configured AI-assisted design system can produce a candidate and a
polished report, a system claim still requires a scoped comparison. The
difference between a plausible candidate and a defensible design is especially
clear here, because the Lighthouse subsystem cannot be judged from one score.
Workload behavior, software support, data movement, physical limits,
verification effort, and deployment conditions can all change which design is
preferable.

Efficiency is a strict claim about how well a particular architecture performs useful work with limited resources. The claim must name the exact design, workload, and resource budget it covers. A faster design fails to solve the problem if it exceeds the power budget, cannot be verified, or depends on fragile software assumptions.

A complete architecture result spans more than efficiency alone. Quantitative
computer architecture treats performance, cost, and power as first-class
concerns [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. The weakening of
Dennard-style scaling, dark silicon, and the limits of multicore scaling made
specialization increasingly important
[@DennardEtAl1974Scaling; @BorkarChien2011FutureMicroprocessors;
@EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon; @JouppiEtAl2017TPU; @ChenEtAl2016Eyeriss; @HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge]. That shift
also made system effects harder to ignore.

Data movement illustrates the broader comparison. In the cited 45\ nm data, a
32-bit integer add costs about 0.1\ pJ, while SRAM and DRAM accesses cost far
more [@Horowitz2014Energy]. The values do not predict a newer process node, but
they explain why an accelerator that adds memory traffic needs a system energy
comparison rather than a compute-only claim. At warehouse scale, the boundary
also includes utilization, networking, power delivery, operations, and total
cost of ownership [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer].
Operational and embodied carbon add assumptions about manufacturing, energy
mix, utilization, geography, and system lifetime [@GuptaEtAl2021ChasingCarbon].
The study should include only the dimensions relevant to its claim and should
name violations, such as design-rule-check (DRC) failures or thermal limits,
that rule out a candidate.

A valid comparison must also account for failed and rejected alternatives, not
only the winners. Keeping those results prevents later architects from
reevaluating candidates that earlier evidence ruled out. It also shows
which parts of the design space the claim actually covers.

Modern benchmark suites already report several dimensions at once. MLPerf Inference,
part of a community effort to make machine-learning performance claims
reproducible across systems, includes deployment scenario, latency, throughput,
and accuracy in its comparisons
[@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf; @ReddiEtAl2020MLPerfInference]. Useful work must be evaluated
against the resource that is scarce in the stated setting, whether that is
latency, throughput, energy, power, area, cost, carbon, reliability,
verification effort, engineering time, or risk.

The design, workload, scenario, and scarce resource together define what
"efficient" means. For the Lighthouse system, a candidate that improves average
throughput may still be a poor choice if it misses an XR frame deadline, exceeds
the 3\ W envelope under sustained load, or adds verification work that the
project cannot absorb. Changing any of those conditions changes the claim and
the evidence needed to support it.

The comparison separates five dimensions of the architecture result from the
cost of the study used to reach it (@tbl-efficiency-dimensions). The first five
rows judge the proposed system. The final row judges the evidence and
engineering effort required to establish the result. An architect should
select the dimensions that define the claim and check where a gain shifts cost
or risk elsewhere.

| **Dimension** | **Question** | **Why it complicates the comparison** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Performance** | How much useful work is delivered per unit time, latency budget, or service-level target? | The answer depends on workload selection, scenario, software stack, and whether the measured behavior matches the deployment claim. |
| **Power and energy** | How much useful work is delivered per watt, joule, thermal budget, or battery envelope? | A credible comparison must account for activity, data movement, voltage/frequency choices, thermal constraints, and fidelity gaps between estimates and signoff. |
| **Reliability and correctness** | Which required behaviors hold across faults, corner cases, nondeterminism, and the declared operating conditions? | A faster candidate is not acceptable if it spends its savings on fragility, security side-channels, debug burden, or invalid software and hardware assumptions. |
| **Scalability and cost** | How much useful work is delivered per dollar, rack, network hop, operator action, or unit of capacity? | Local wins can shift cost to memory, network, power delivery, utilization, operations, or total cost of ownership. |
| **Sustainability** | How much useful work is delivered per unit of operational and embodied environmental footprint? | Carbon depends on hardware lifetime, manufacturing, energy mix, utilization, and where and when computation runs. |
| **Study cost: evidence and engineering effort** | How much decision-relevant evidence is obtained per simulation, experiment, verification run, or engineer-hour? | Generating more candidates can still be inefficient if evaluation consumes scarce feedback, hides failures, or cannot reject weak outputs. |

: **A system result and the work needed to establish it require different measures.** Five dimensions describe the proposed system, while evidence and engineering effort describe the study. A valid comparison must show when an apparent improvement shifts cost or changes the scope. {#tbl-efficiency-dimensions tbl-colwidths="[22,32,34]"}

Reducing the cost of the study is valuable only when the remaining observations can still distinguish the alternatives and expose the failures that matter to the decision.

These dimensions interact. In the mobile XR setting anchored by XRBench and ILLIXR, frame latency, energy, sustained power, and data movement are so tightly coupled that a gain in one can violate a deadline or thermal limit in another. Better simulated performance can be offset by added verification work, and lower energy may depend on fragile software assumptions. A candidate that wins under a proxy may fail on a more faithful workload. The architect must explain which tradeoffs are acceptable for the stated constraints, defining the scope of the system claim instead of relying on a single attractive artifact or score.

These coupled requirements do not imply that every architecture project needs
AI. Conventional architecture methods may remain preferable when the design
question and permitted change are narrow enough to evaluate directly and the
required feedback is cheap and dependable. We should first identify what
familiar models, scripts, simulators, and expert reviews already handle well
before stating exactly what we expect AI to improve. The test is whether the
assistance leads to a better system or a more reliable conclusion, rather than
simply generating more artifacts.

Measured RTL-generation benchmarks report substantial functional-test failures
among generated candidates, which makes independent checks essential
[@VerilogEval; @PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval]. The practical question
is whether the complete approach and its required checks improve the
architecture result, lower the
total cost of reaching a result of comparable quality, or both, relative to
competent conventional work. If every bad proposal requires a multi-hour
synthesis run, evaluation can consume more engineering time and computation
than the method saves.

The Lighthouse prompt makes this friction concrete. The requested subsystem must support a workload class, meet a strict power envelope, fit a technology assumption, interact correctly with software, and produce reviewable evidence. The final comparison must weigh energy, latency, memory traffic, programmability, verification, and deployment risk. While a single scalar objective may help an automated search navigate the space, it cannot substitute for architectural judgment.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
```

## What Current Systems Establish

The public examples reviewed through July 2026 establish individual
capabilities rather than an end-to-end answer. Their strongest claims become
clearer when the check behind each result is explicit. For each system, the
relevant questions are what artifact or result it produced, what check could
reject it, how much of the architecture problem that check observes, and what
an outside reviewer can inspect. Following those checks reveals both the
progress and the remaining gap without treating unlike systems as steps in a
single ranking.

Exact or inexpensive checks can support strong claims over a narrow task.
AlphaTensor found a 4 by 4 matrix-multiplication algorithm over the field of
two elements that uses 47 scalar multiplications rather than Strassen's 49
[@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor]. Every candidate admitted an exact algebraic check.
AutoTVM similarly evaluates many tensor-program schedules on real hardware,
where the result is measurable and most failures remain inside the tuning run
[@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. These checks make search practical, but neither result
establishes a complete system architecture.

Proxy and simulator feedback support broader exploration but inherit the
limits of the model doing the checking. AlphaChip uses wirelength and congestion
proxies to guide macro placement [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. ArchGym found
that no search algorithm dominates across design spaces when simulators and
sample budgets are held fixed [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. Apollo reduces costly
target evaluations by transferring knowledge across related accelerator design
spaces, while BOOM-Explorer pays hours per sample for a documented 7\ nm flow
[@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer]. Each result is meaningful
within its feedback source, and each requires stronger evidence before it can
support a wider physical or system claim.

Functional tests, post-synthesis metrics, and fabricated silicon establish
different levels of hardware progress. Functional success alone does not
establish hardware design quality. VerilogEval checks functional behavior
[@VerilogEval; @PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval], while RTLLM adds
post-synthesis design-quality measures without reaching physical signoff
[@RTLLM].
Chip-Chat reached tapeout for a small processor through extensive human-guided
revision, and Enlightenment-1 produced a fabricated RISC-V core through an
automated iterative verification-and-revision loop
[@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat; @ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU]. These are substantial
implementation results, but neither establishes the full multi-tool
system-architecture capability posed by the moonshot.

Human ratings and proprietary deployment reports are harder to evaluate from
outside. ChipNeMo reports task-specific internal gains, ChatEDA checks tool
execution and human-rated request fulfillment on 50 ChatEDA-Bench tasks using a
simplified OpenROAD wrapper, and DSO.ai
reports 100 commercial tapeouts without a public matched methodology
[@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @HeEtAl2024ChatEDA; @Synopsys2023DSOai]. These reports
show that learned methods are entering real workflows. They do not by
themselves establish independent functional correctness, complete physical
signoff, or a net benefit over a strong alternative.

These examples demonstrate useful pieces of a broader design
capability. Learned search and measured autotuning can explore choices,
placement and RTL generation can produce artifacts, tool-using systems can
invoke real flows, domain adaptation can support selected engineering tasks,
and generated designs can reach silicon under bounded conditions. The
moonshot is to connect such demonstrated capabilities through current project
state and appropriate design tools while retaining independent checks that can
reject an unsound result. No one example yet establishes that complete system.

Across these systems, a result supports only the claim made inspectable by its
check. Check cost and fidelity, task scope, baseline quality, workflow coverage,
and access to supporting material each limit what an architect can conclude
(@tbl-existing-systems).

| **System** | **What it establishes** | **The telltale limit** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AlphaTensor [@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor] | Learned search improved a fifty-year-old matrix-multiplication count for 4 by 4 matrices over the field of two elements | The finite-field construction admits an exact algebraic check, and one scalar scores it |
| AutoTVM [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM] | Measured search can improve schedules when many candidates run quickly on real hardware | The result covers tensor-program schedules, where failures are usually contained within the tuning run |
| AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment] | A learned policy produces macro placements a production flow accepts | The reward is proxy wirelength and congestion, and the matched baseline is disputed |
| ArchGym [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym] | At equal sample budgets no search algorithm dominates, so the harness and budget shape the result | Every candidate is graded by a simulator, so the result inherits its fidelity limits |
| Apollo and BOOM-Explorer [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer] | Learned design-space exploration can exploit domain-specific evidence | Apollo transfers across related accelerator spaces to reduce costly target evaluations; BOOM-Explorer uses an open-source core but depends on commercial tools and pays hours per sample |
| VerilogEval and RTLLM [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM] | RTL generation is measurable on shared tasks | VerilogEval emphasizes functional simulation; RTLLM adds post-synthesis quality metrics; neither reaches physical signoff |
| Chip-Chat and Enlightenment-1 [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat; @ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU] | Generated logic has reached silicon, in one case a core that boots Linux | One depends on extensive human-guided revision; the other demonstrates an automated processor implementation and verification loop, not the full multi-tool system-architecture capability posed by the moonshot |
| ChatEDA [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA] | An agent can plan and invoke a real tool flow from stated intent | The benchmark checks tool execution and human-rated request fulfillment on 50 ChatEDA-Bench tasks using a simplified OpenROAD wrapper, not independent functional correctness or complete signoff |
| ChipNeMo [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo] | Domain adaptation can improve selected internal engineering tasks | The gains are task-specific, general models remain stronger on some subtasks, and the proprietary evaluation is not externally reproducible |
| DSO.ai [@Synopsys2023DSOai] | Learned flow-parameter search has reached 100 vendor-reported commercial tapeouts | The evidence standard is a press release, with no public methodology or matched baseline |

: **The strength of each result depends on its scope and how it was evaluated:** Exact, inexpensive checks support strong scoped claims, while narrow measurements, proxies, weak baselines, and supporting data, methods, or artifacts that outsiders cannot inspect each limit what an architect can conclude. {#tbl-existing-systems tbl-colwidths="[20,37,43]"}

The table is a set of scoped claims, not a ranking of systems. Shared tasks can
make it easier to inspect where each claim stops.
ImageNet [@RussakovskyEtAl2015ImageNet] provided computer vision with a common
benchmark, while CASP (Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction)
[@MoultEtAl1995CASP] let AlphaFold's [@JumperEtAl2021AlphaFold] structure
predictions face a community-held assessment. These precedents demonstrate the
value of common tasks and checks. They do not remove the need to qualify what a
domain-specific check establishes.

Software engineering offers a useful contrast because a public test harness can
often return a task-level result much faster than hardware design can obtain
physical evidence. SWE-bench turns real GitHub-issue fixes into a shared task
graded by automated repository tests, giving coding systems a relatively quick
and repeatable signal (@fig-swebench-progress) [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench].
Passing those tests supports a claim about resolving the issue under the
benchmark conditions, not complete software correctness. Hardware also has
fast checks for specific properties, but a complete system-and-chip claim must
connect functional verification with synthesis, timing, power, physical-design,
and thermal evidence whose cost and fidelity differ.

```{python}
#| label: fig-swebench-progress
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Standardized task-level checks support rapid iteration on SWE-bench Verified.** SWE-bench Verified defines a human-validated 500-instance subset [@OpenAI2024SWEBenchVerified]. A later OpenAI audit reported flawed tests and contamination and no longer recommended SWE-bench Verified for frontier capability measurement [@OpenAI2026SWEBenchLimits]. The plotted values come from a frozen July 19, 2026, dataset-transcribed snapshot of Epoch AI's model database, whose documentation describes a daily-updated dataset [@EpochAI2025AIModels]. The line traces the best reported resolved rate in that snapshot, from roughly 31 percent to 83 percent in about seventeen months. The retained receipt contains model names, release dates, and resolved fractions, not a controlled evaluation protocol, so the plot shows the reported trend rather than a controlled comparison among models or systems. Repository tests provide a quick, repeatable signal for the defined task, while a complete architecture claim must combine functional and physical evidence from several tools.
#| out-width: "88%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter of the best reported SWE-bench Verified resolved percentage for each model name versus model release date from late 2024 to 2026. Points climb from about 31 percent to about 83 percent, with a solid line tracing the best-to-date frontier."

import csv
import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Data: Dataset-transcribed snapshot of values labeled as SWE-bench Verified in
# Epoch AI's model database [@EpochAI2025AIModels]; best reported value per
# model name in the retained snapshot. Accessed 2026-07-19. The database
# documentation does not independently verify each plotted value.
# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter1-swebench-verified.csv
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

def _yfrac(text):
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%d", "%Y-%m", "%Y"):
        try:
            d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text.strip(), fmt)
            return d.year + (d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1) / 365.25
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return None

pts = []
with open(_root / "data" / "source-receipts" / "chapter1-swebench-verified.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    for row in csv.DictReader(fh):
        x = _yfrac(row["release_date"])
        try:
            score = float(row["resolved_fraction"])
        except ValueError:
            continue
        if x is None:
            continue
        pts.append({"model": row["model"], "score": score * 100 if score <= 1 else score, "x": x})

# The snapshot contains repeated rows under some model names. Retain only the
# best reported value for each name rather than presenting those rows as
# distinct model releases.
best_by_name = {}
for p in pts:
    name = (p["model"] or "").strip()
    if name not in best_by_name or p["score"] > best_by_name[name]["score"]:
        best_by_name[name] = p
pts = list(best_by_name.values())
pts.sort(key=lambda p: p["x"])
best = -1.0
frontier = []
for p in pts:
    if p["score"] > best:
        best = p["score"]
        frontier.append(p)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 3.2))
ax.scatter([p["x"] for p in pts], [p["score"] for p in pts], s=16, marker="o",
           facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.7, zorder=2, label="Named models")
ax.plot([p["x"] for p in frontier], [p["score"] for p in frontier], color=COLORS["evidence"], lw=1.6, zorder=3)
ax.scatter([p["x"] for p in frontier], [p["score"] for p in frontier], s=22, marker="o",
           facecolor=COLORS["evidence"], edgecolor=COLORS["evidence_ink"], linewidth=0.5, zorder=4, label="Best to date")
ax.set_xlim(2024.8, 2026.55)
ax.set_ylim(20, 92)
ax.set_xlabel("Model release date", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("SWE-bench Verified resolved (%)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([2025.0, 2025.5, 2026.0, 2026.5])
ax.set_xticklabels(["2025", "mid-25", "2026", "mid-26"], fontsize=6.4)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.4, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="y", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=6.0, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.10, right=0.97, top=0.98, bottom=0.12)
```

The trend does not isolate model, harness, or system effects
(@fig-swebench-progress), because the retained receipt records reported values
rather than a controlled evaluation protocol and a later OpenAI audit withdrew
SWE-bench Verified from frontier capability measurement
[@OpenAI2026SWEBenchLimits]. It still demonstrates how a standardized, automated
task-level check can support rapid iteration across models and engineering
systems. Architecture also uses fast analytical, structural, and functional
checks, but no single one closes a complete
system-and-chip claim. Early screens may leave timing, design-rule, power, and
thermal feasibility estimated or untested. A physical-feasibility claim
eventually requires the relevant implementation-facing checks. Static analysis
and calibrated proxies can reduce their cost by screening candidates, but they
cannot replace them.

Architecture already has shared checks at individual layers. SPEC-style
benchmarks made performance claims more comparable through common workloads,
run rules, and reporting standards, while also steering which improvements the
community pursues [@Patterson2012Benchmarks; @SPEC2017CPU]. gem5 and FireSim
provide shared simulation platforms at different costs and fidelities
[@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5; @KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. MLPerf defines benchmark
suites and submission rules for machine-learning systems
[@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. These resources demonstrate that outside researchers
can rerun, compare, and challenge a scoped result. They do not make the result
automatically correct or connect all the evidence required for the Lighthouse.
Current systems therefore establish bounded progress toward the moonshot, not
an end-to-end verdict.

## Scarce Architecture Data and Costly Verification {#sec-data-scarcity-verification-load}

The moonshot depends on scarce project-specific information that connects an
architecture choice to a physical result. It also depends on enough
verification capacity to test candidates after they are produced.

Public software repositories can expose source changes, technical discussion,
and tests. ChipNeMo, for example, draws on proprietary software, RTL,
verification testbenches, specifications, and documentation
[@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. For an architecture study, a model trained on public text
may produce plausible RTL while missing the project's interface, PDK, memory, or
signoff constraints. Open designs and open PDKs are valuable, but they do not
substitute for the authorized PDK, IP, and tool configuration of the project
whose physical claim is being evaluated.

Technical fit is not the only condition on usable project data. A candidate
must also survive legal and compliance checks. If a model generates RTL by
regurgitating code from its training set without strict provenance tracking,
that candidate risks inbound IP contamination. Conversely, sending proprietary
specifications, constraints, or EDA tool reports to an unauthorized model
endpoint creates an outbound disclosure risk. Without strict provenance and
isolation, an AI-generated architecture cannot pass legal signoff, negating
any speedup gained during candidate production. Source permission, generated-output
provenance, project confidentiality, and outside-review access remain separate
conditions on data use and review.

The missing information need not come from training data alone. Architects can
supply specifications and analytical models, encode machine-checkable
constraints, retrieve current documentation, and use tool returns to revise a
candidate. RTLFixer demonstrates tool-guided repair after syntax and compiler
feedback [@TsaiEtAl2024RTLFixer]. Chipyard connects shareable RISC-V designs to
simulation and implementation paths [@chipyard], while OpenROAD provides an
open digital physical-design flow [@AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD]. These resources
demonstrate useful ways to expose constraints and feedback. They do not recover
the proprietary information outside their coverage. The mechanisms for
building and representing project knowledge belong to
@sec-data-representations-world-models.

Candidate production also leaves verification in place. A first-pass RTL
candidate can be plausible and subtly wrong.
The cited industry survey reports that verification consumes roughly half of
total project engineering effort, with design engineers spending about half
their time in verification [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. A reusable
UVM[^fn-uvm-c01] environment can serve many related candidates, but its
stimulus, checkers, assertions, coverage model, and debug capacity must still
keep pace with the behaviors those candidates introduce. When candidate
production outruns that capacity, the limiting work has moved to verification.
Faster generation is useful only if the project can still reject bad candidates
at the required rate and fidelity.

[^fn-uvm-c01]: **UVM (Universal Verification Methodology)**: A standardized methodology and class library for building reusable SystemVerilog verification environments, including stimulus, monitors, scoreboards, and coverage components [@IEEE2020UVM].

Verification must also reach past functional correctness when the design's threat model includes hardware security. Spectre showed that functionally correct processors can still expose microarchitectural side channels [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. An AI-assisted study that generates security-relevant hardware must apply independent checks appropriate to the design and threat model, which may include isolation properties, side-channel analysis, or checks for malicious modifications. Generation may help produce SystemVerilog assertions, security properties, and testbenches, but it does not establish its own correctness.

Scarce project information and costly verification make explicit state a
requirement for AI-assisted architecture. Automated components need the
current candidate, constraints, permitted actions, and tool returns in a
machine-usable form. Reviewers need the measurements, failed checks, and
assumptions required to judge the resulting recommendation. This does not replace
established architecture practice. It changes what that practice must expose
when learned methods participate.

## Architecture 2.0 Extends Established Practice {#sec-from-architecture-10-to-architecture-20}

Architecture 1.0 is shorthand for established, human-directed architecture
practice. It already includes analytical models, scripted flows, automated
search, parameterized generators, simulators, synthesis, optimization, and
verification. Architecture 2.0 retains that foundation while allowing learned
methods to perform selected roles across more of the work
[@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. The distinction is about the breadth
and role of AI participation, not manual work versus automation
(@tbl-arch1-vs-arch2).

| **Feature** | **Established architecture practice (Architecture 1.0)** | **AI-assisted architecture practice (Architecture 2.0)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem framing | Architects define the question, abstractions, constraints, and tool tasks | Learned methods may help interpret broader intent or incomplete information and propose choices for architect review |
| Exploration | Architects use analytical models, scripts, parameterized generators, sweeps, and conventional optimization | Prediction, generation, and learned optimization may propose, screen, or select alternatives alongside established methods |
| Tool use | Architects and scripts invoke simulators and design tools, preserve results, and decide what to run next | Automated components may select later actions from tool returns, so state, cost, failures, and permitted actions must be usable by the component and inspectable by the reviewer |
| Result standard | Measurements and checks turn candidate artifacts into comparisons that can support the next architecture action | The same standard applies; broader automated participation does not make an unchecked artifact an architecture result |
| Recommendation and commitment | Architects integrate results and form the technical recommendation; a named commitment authority decides whether the architecture advances to the next consequential transition | Methods may organize analysis or prepare a draft recommendation, while the architect and commitment authority retain their respective responsibilities |

: **AI participation broadens what may be delegated without changing the authority structure.** Architecture 2.0 adds learned prediction, generation, optimization, retrieval, or tool coordination to established analytical and automated practice while the architect retains the technical recommendation and a named commitment authority decides whether the architecture advances to the next consequential transition. {#tbl-arch1-vs-arch2}

AI participation does not create explicit evidence or sound record keeping.
Conventional projects can already preserve requirements, artifact versions,
tool databases, verification results, rejected candidates, and decisions.
Project knowledge and state are often distributed across those engineering
artifacts and expert practice. When automated components participate, the
selected state and permitted actions they use must additionally be represented
for machine use while remaining inspectable by reviewers
(@fig-design-loop-breaks).

![**Automated participation adds a machine-use requirement.** Established architecture work can retain explicit evidence while project knowledge remains distributed across specifications, source, tool databases, verification artifacts, and expert practice. When automated components participate, selected state and permitted actions must additionally be represented for machine use while remaining inspectable by reviewers. Both panels retain a review point and a feedback path; neither assigns organizational commitment to that review step.](images/F2a-design-loop-breaks){#fig-design-loop-breaks width="85%" fig-alt="Two side-by-side diagrams compare established human-orchestrated and AI-assisted architecture studies. The left distributes project knowledge across engineering artifacts, records, and expert practice. The right additionally represents selected state and permitted actions for automated methods. Both panels retain explicit evidence, expert or architect review, and a feedback path without assigning organizational commitment to the review step."}

Machine-usable state must remain aligned with the artifacts and records that
reviewers inspect. This requirement neither validates the outputs nor transfers
the technical recommendation or commitment authority.

## Coordinating Methods, Tools, and Independent Checks

Deliberate coordination must keep every local action tied to the original
design question. Otherwise a generator, surrogate, simulator, or implementation
tool can succeed locally while advancing the wrong candidate or omitting a
system obligation.

The design system keeps the architecture question and its obligations current
alongside candidate, tool, and version state. It then assigns prediction,
generation, optimization, or conventional methods according to the work that
is limiting. Tool feedback and independent checks constrain their outputs,
while cost and stopping conditions bound the work.

Candidate production must remain separate enough from checking to expose
failure. Nominally independent implementations can fail on the same
hard inputs [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion], and several components may repeat
the same wrong assumption when they share training data, a proxy, or an
underlying model. This book uses *independent check* as an operational
threshold: the producing method neither controls the check nor serves as its
sole pass/fail authority, and the check's decisive assumptions and
implementation are not inherited unchanged from the generator. Complete
independence is uncommon, but a check that only repeats the producer's
assumptions cannot qualify the result.

Even a well-coordinated study cannot establish whether the proposed
architecture succeeds or whether the complete approach improves the
work. Those judgments require separate tests.

## Two Independent Tests for the Moonshot

The first test evaluates the architecture. The second evaluates the effect of
the complete human-plus-technical approach.

**Architecture result.** Does the study establish whether any proposed design
meets the fixed Lighthouse conditions and justifies itself against the
architecture reference under the required workload, software, implementation,
physical, and verification checks? The result may establish that one design is
better, support a recommendation to retain the reference, or find that the
available alternatives do not meet the conditions.

**Complete AI-assisted approach.** Against the strongest practical
conventional or human-directed workflow with matched starting information,
tool access, total budget, human work accounting, and stopping conditions, did
the complete approach improve the architecture result, reduce the total cost
of reaching a result of comparable quality, or both?

The distinction has several consequences. A good design does not prove that
the complete approach improved the work. A cheaper process does not justify an
inferior design. A sound conventional result remains a success for the
architecture question even if the complete approach is not better. Random
search may provide a useful floor, but it is not automatically the strongest
practical conventional comparison.

Neither comparison identifies the contribution of a named foundation model,
generator, surrogate, or other component. That narrower claim requires a
controlled replacement or ablation within an otherwise matched system.
"Independent" here means that the two tests answer different questions, not
that their measurements are statistically independent.

A broader program assessment aggregates repeated comparisons of the complete
approach across tasks, design stages, and conditions rather than adding a third
test. Program-level success requires the complete approach to improve
architecture results, reduce the total cost of reaching results of comparable
quality, or both across the declared scope. The public evidence reviewed for
this edition does not yet settle that verdict.

One successful Lighthouse study would be an existence proof, not broad
validation of a new design method. The same two tests must hold across declared
tasks and conditions. Independent teams must be able to reproduce the relevant
measurements or supported results from the preserved inputs, tools, and checks.
They must also inspect the basis for the technical recommendation.

## Common Pitfalls

When adopting AI-assisted methods or evaluating moonshot proposals, it is easy to conflate a local win with a system victory. The following pitfalls highlight where unverified assumptions, misapplied metrics, or incomplete boundaries lead to flawed architectural conclusions:

**Confusing Artifacts with Results.** Mistaking a generated block of RTL or a syntactically correct script for an architecture decision. A valid result must be checked against workload, software, and physical constraints before it can support a commitment.

**Ignoring the System Boundary.** Optimizing an isolated component, such as an accelerator, without accounting for data movement, memory bandwidth limits, or strict interface constraints (like AXI handshakes). A faster block that violates system integration is not a solution.

**Overfitting to Proxies.** Using surrogate models or fast proxy metrics to repeatedly optimize a design, only to find the "gains" disappear when subjected to higher-fidelity verification tools. Proxy exploitation creates an illusion of progress that physical tools overturn.

**Conflating Method Success with Architecture Success.** Celebrating a fast AI-assisted generation step even if the total end-to-end cost (including verification and human review) is higher, or the final architecture is inferior. The method's speed does not automatically justify the resulting architecture.

## Open Questions

The moonshot opens questions that no single design study can settle. Every
